In its place came a new concern with single-page illustrations, such as this one, which have no specific content or meaning. THE HOLDING MUSEUM'S METADATA
  title:            Pot
  description:      Within the Zulu culture (the Northern Nguni tribe), the making of beer pots is the traditional function of women. A potter will travel far searching in riverbeds or for anthills that can supply the correct clay for the vessels. Formed using the coil technique and smoothed using flattened stones, the pots are fired in a dug-out earthen "kiln," and covered with palm leaves, whose oil results in the blackened, shiny texture of the vessels. Years of use deepen this texture to a rich woody patina.
  location on file: Southern Africa, South Africa, Zulu-style potter  (held by: Cleveland Museum of Art)

THE HOLDING MUSEUM'S METADATA
  title:            Turkmen Main Carpet
  description:      In the Islamic world, carpets symbolize status and wealth. A carpet’s origin can be identified by its design, color, and technique. Shades of red and lobed motifs, or guls, are hallmarks of Turkmen carpets woven by nomadic tribes across northeast Iran, Afghanistan, and central Asia. This main carpet of the Yomud tribe features beautiful colors in the guls on a rich aubergine ground; the decorated skirts, or elem, with stylized flora at each end, are its rarest feature. This carpet would have been the prized possession within the living quarters of a round tent, or yurt.

  title:            Statuette of Kneeling King
  description:      As the chief intermediary between gods and men, the Egyptian king is often shown kneeling in adoration.   title:            Tanbūr
  description:      This long-necked lute collected in Ottoman Syria possesses traits that are Syrian, Turkish, and Iranian and provides an example of the musical interaction between cultures. It is often used as a solo instrument in both sacred and secular contexts. Burn marks decorate the pear-shaped body along with inlaid dots of mother-of-pearl, which may also have helped with navigation of the fret board by the player.

  description:      Carved out of ivory or wood in a variety of shapes, Chokwe whistles often bear miniature, stylized renderings of masks.   title:            gown; tobe
  description:      Man’s gown (boubou, tobe, riga), hand-woven from hand-spun white cotton. The body is formed of 163 narrow strips hand-sewn together along the selvedges vertically, while the sleeves are sewn horizontally. The body of the gown is rectangular in shape, while the sleeves flare out at the top being wider at the top than at the bottom. At the front is sewn a large pocket. The pocket and gown are hand-embroidered in the ‘two knives’ (aska biyu) pattern using a beige local silk thread (tsamiya or sanyan) and chain and buttonhole eyelet stitching. The neck and sleeves of the garment are hemmed.

THE HOLDING MUSEUM'S METADATA
  title:            Talatat: Portrait of Nefertiti
  description:      The son of Amenhotep III, Akhenaten, brought about the short-lived "monotheistic" revolution in Egyptian religion near the end of Dynasty 18. The young king constructed a temple complex to the Aten, the Sun Disk, at Karnak—from which this relief comes—before he moved his capital to El Armana. For reasons yet unknown, the figure of the Queen Nefertiti appears in these reliefs far more often than that of the king. Ironically, the Aten temples were dismantled anciently to be used as foundations and fill for additions to the Great Temple of Amun, whom the Aten had briefly displaced.
